opus-5.5.text:
I think the central challenge is the gap between what a benchmark measures and what we actually care about when an agent is deployed in the real world. With simulated benchmarks, you're constructing an artificial environment, a set of tasks, and some way of scoring success, and every one of those choices bakes in assumptions that may not hold once the agent is out there interacting with messy, open-ended situations.

A few things make this especially hard for agents compared to, say, classic language model evaluation. First, agents take actions with consequences, so it's not enough to ask whether the final answer is right. You care about cost, about whether the agent did something irreversible or harmful along the way, about whether it asked for clarification when it should have. Most benchmarks collapse all of that into a single accuracy number, and that hides a lot.

Second, there's the cost issue, which I think has been badly neglected. You can often boost an agent's benchmark score just by running it many times, retrying, or using a much more expensive model under the hood. If leaderboards report only accuracy and not the dollars spent to get there, you end up rewarding approaches that aren't practical, and you can't tell whether a fancy new agent architecture is actually better than a simple baseline that just retries a few times.

Third, there's overfitting and shortcuts. Benchmarks are static, developers iterate against them, and agents are very good at finding ways to succeed on the benchmark that don't generalize. Sometimes the holdout sets are inadequate or nonexistent, so you can't distinguish genuine capability from tuning to the test.

And finally, there's the question of who the evaluation is for. A model developer wants to know whether their research direction is working. A downstream developer wants to know whether this agent will do their specific job reliably and cheaply. Those are different questions, and a single benchmark usually can't answer both well.

So my overall view is that we need to treat agent evaluation much more like we treat evaluating any product or system meant for real use: report costs alongside accuracy, use proper holdouts, look at reliability and not just peak performance, and complement simulated benchmarks with evidence from actual deployments. Otherwise there's a real risk that impressive benchmark numbers create a misleading picture of how capable and useful these agents actually are.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can succeed on static benchmarks through overfitting or shortcuts that do not generalize, creating a misleading picture of their usefulness in real-world deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the central challenge is that simulated benchmarks ask a question that's different from the one we actually care about. The benchmark asks, "Can the agent complete this task in this environment?" The question we care about is, "Will this agent do useful work for real people in the messy world?" And those two things can come apart in ways that are surprisingly hard to detect.

Let me unpack that a bit. When you build a simulated environment, you have to make a huge number of choices about what to include and what to abstract away. You decide what the websites look like, what the APIs return, what the edge cases are, how the "user" behaves. Every one of those choices is a simplification, and agents are extraordinarily good at exploiting simplifications. Not necessarily in a malicious way, just in the sense that an agent optimized against a benchmark will find whatever regularities exist in that benchmark, and those regularities often don't exist in the real world. So you end up with a kind of construct validity problem. The thing you're measuring isn't quite the thing you think you're measuring.

The second piece is that agents operate over long horizons with many steps, and that changes the nature of evaluation. With a language model, you ask a question, you get an answer, you can check it. With an agent, there are many ways to arrive at a correct final state, and many of them involve doing something you'd never want in practice. Deleting files, spending money, taking shortcuts that happen to work. If your benchmark only checks the end state, you can have an agent that scores well and is actually quite dangerous to deploy. So we need to evaluate the process, not just the outcome, and that's much harder to do in a scalable way.

The third piece is cost, and this is something I've been pretty vocal about. A lot of agent leaderboards report accuracy and nothing else. But you can almost always buy more accuracy by spending more. Run the agent ten times and take a majority vote, use a bigger model, add more reflection steps. If the leaderboard doesn't account for that, it rewards approaches that would be totally impractical to deploy. So we've argued that agent evaluation needs to be at least two-dimensional, accuracy and cost, and ideally you're looking at the Pareto frontier rather than a single number.

And then finally there's the contamination and overfitting issue. Simulated benchmarks tend to be small, they're static, and once they're public, they get optimized against directly, sometimes inadvertently. Developers run hundreds of experiments against the same test set. In some cases the training data of the models includes the benchmark or near copies of it. So the numbers go up, but the capability may not be moving as much as it appears.

I want to be clear that I'm not saying simulated benchmarks are useless. They're necessary. You can't run every experiment on live systems with real users. But I think we have to be a lot more humble about what they tell us, invest much more in holdout sets and in evaluations that resemble deployment conditions, and be honest in how we report results. Right now there's a big gap between the rhetoric around agent capabilities and what the evidence actually supports, and the way we do evaluation is a big part of why that gap exists.

r001.rationale: The response explains that agents can exploit benchmark simplifications and score well on simulated tasks without performing useful work in the real world, so benchmark success may not transfer to deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is whether success in the simulation translates into success in the real world. You can make a benchmark very reproducible, with a clear task and an automatic way to score the outcome, but those choices can also remove precisely the things that make real tasks difficult: ambiguity, missing information, and the need to interact with people.

So an agent might score very well because it’s adapted to the assumptions of that simulated environment. That doesn’t necessarily tell us whether it can handle the task a user actually cares about. And as we optimize against the benchmark, that gap can grow.

The question we need to ask is: What evidence do we have that this benchmark measures the capability we intend it to measure? That requires validating the simulation against real tasks and real outcomes. Otherwise, we have a precise measurement, but we don’t necessarily know what it means.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can score well by adapting to the simulation’s assumptions, without demonstrating they can handle real user tasks, and that optimizing the benchmark can widen this transfer gap.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is whether success in the simulation translates into success in the real world. You can build a benchmark that’s reproducible and easy to score, but in doing that, you often strip away the things that make a task difficult in practice: ambiguous goals, incomplete information, changing environments, and interactions with other people.

So an agent might do very well on the benchmark by exploiting regularities in the simulated environment, without developing the capabilities you actually care about. And if you’re only measuring whether it completed the task, you can miss how much it cost, how much human intervention it needed, or whether it made mistakes along the way.

The question is really: What does this benchmark give us evidence for? A high score can be useful, but we need to validate the connection between that score and reliable performance in the setting where we want to deploy the agent.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can score well by exploiting simulated regularities without developing the capabilities needed for real-world performance, and calls for validating transfer to deployment.
